formation.title: The Birth of Spain
formation.text:
The crowns are united, the Moors driven from their last stronghold, and the banner of Spain flies over lands our ancestors could scarcely imagine. In Seville and Valladolid, in Barcelona and Toledo, the peoples of Iberia look to a common destiny. Yet the path forward divides before us. Shall Spain be the sword of Catholic Europe, our tercios the terror of heretics and infidels, our Inquisition the guarantor of orthodoxy, our king the champion of a universal Christian order? Or shall we look westward, where our caravels have found a New World of unimaginable riches, building not merely a kingdom but a global empire of commerce, colonies, and treasure fleets that will make Seville the center of the world?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the sword of Christendom.

modifiers.name: Universal Monarchy
modifiers.text: Spain stands as the champion of Christendom, its tercios the finest soldiers in Europe and its faith the unshakeable foundation of a world-spanning empire.

options.text: The wealth of the Indies shall be ours.

modifiers.name: Empire of the Indies
modifiers.text: From Seville to Manila, Spain's fleets bind together a global commercial empire, its harbors teeming with the wealth of two hemispheres.

advances.name: Alcazars of the Crown
advances.text: The royal alcazars of Segovia, Toledo and Seville are palace and fortress in one, taken over from Moorish builders and garrisoned in the king's name inside the cities themselves.

advances.name: Merino Flocks
advances.text: The flocks of Castile winter in Extremadura and La Mancha and summer in the mountains of León and Soria, walking the royal drove roads between them. Their fine short fleece has no equal in Europe, and the sheep that bear it may not be taken out of the kingdom.

advances.name: Iberian Military Orders
advances.text: The Orders of Santiago, Calatrava, and Alcantara, warrior-monks who held the frontier and whose Grand Masters commanded vast estates and loyal levies.

advances.name: Fueros and Cortes
advances.text: The fueros grant local liberties and privileges, while the Cortes assemblies of Castile, Aragon, and Catalonia give voice to the estates of the realm.

advances.name: Jinete Tradition
advances.text: The jinetes, light cavalrymen riding a la jineta with short stirrups and light lances, are the quintessential Iberian horsemen, heirs to a tradition shared between Christian and Moorish riders.

advances.name: Burgos Wool Market
advances.text: The great wool fairs of Burgos channel Castilian merino fleece to the looms of Flanders and Italy, making wool Spain's first great export commodity.

advances.name: The Catholic Monarchs
advances.text: Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile united the crowns, subdued the nobility, reformed the administration, and set Spain on the path to empire.

advances.name: Reconquista Culmination
advances.text: The fall of Granada in 1492 completed the centuries-long Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule.

effects.name: War Score vs other Religion Efficiency

event.title: The Fall of Granada
event.text: On the second day of January, Boabdil, the last Emir of Granada, surrendered the keys of the Alhambra to the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella. Seven centuries of Reconquista are complete. The Moorish crescent has been struck from every tower in Iberia, replaced by the cross and the banner of Castile and Aragon. In the streets of Granada, the faithful celebrate with processions and Te Deums. Yet amid the jubilation, a question lingers. The conquered Moorish and Jewish populations possess skills, knowledge, and trading networks that have enriched Iberia for generations. Shall we forge ahead with religious purity, expelling or converting all who do not share the true faith, or preserve the intellectual heritage of convivencia, the tradition of coexistence that made Al-Andalus a beacon of learning?

options.text: Purity of faith above all else.

modifiers.name: Reconquista Triumphant
modifiers.text: The seven-hundred-year struggle for Iberia is won. Christian arms have prevailed, and the fervor of the crusade burns bright.

modifiers.name: Legacy of Convivencia
modifiers.text: Centuries of coexistence between Christian, Muslim, and Jewish communities have left Spain a reservoir of diverse knowledge and cultural sophistication.

advances.name: The Spanish Inquisition
advances.text: Established in 1478, the Inquisition served as the Crown's instrument for enforcing religious conformity and rooting out heresy, extending its reach across all Spanish territories.

advances.name: Iberian Exploration
advances.text: Spanish navigators pushed beyond the known world, Columbus westward, Magellan around the globe, guided by advances in cartography, astronomy, and shipbuilding.

advances.name: Medina del Campo Fairs
advances.text: The great fairs of Medina del Campo drew merchants from across Europe, becoming one of the continent's premier centers for banking, exchange, and international commerce.

advances.name: Rise of the Tercio
advances.text: The tercio, Spain's revolutionary combined-arms infantry formation of pikemen, swordsmen, and arquebusiers, dominated European battlefields from Cerignola to Rocroi.

event.title: The Great Captain's Revolution
event.text: In the Italian Wars, Gonzalo Fernandez de Cordoba, El Gran Capitan, has transformed the art of warfare. Where other armies rely on masses of pikemen or expensive mercenary cavalry, Cordoba has forged a new kind of formation: the tercio. Three thousand men, pikemen, swordsmen armed with the fearsome espada ropera, and arquebusiers, drill together as a single combined-arms unit. At Cerignola in 1503, this revolutionary formation shattered the French gendarmerie, proving that disciplined infantry could defeat the finest heavy cavalry in Europe. The tercio will dominate European battlefields for the next century and a half. Shall we perfect the tercio as a combined-arms instrument of shock and discipline, or hone it for the long marches and distant campaigns that Spain's sprawling empire demands?

options.text: Perfect the art of combined arms.

modifiers.name: Tercio: Combined Arms Doctrine
modifiers.text: The tercio fights as a single organism, pikemen shielding arquebusiers, swordsmen closing the gaps, each man trusting the formation with his life.

options.text: Forge soldiers who can fight anywhere.

modifiers.name: Tercio: Expeditionary Doctrine
modifiers.text: Spain's tercios have learned to fight far from home, in the swamps of Flanders, the mountains of Italy, the forests of the New World, adapting their tactics to every terrain.

advances.name: Colonial Trade Infrastructure
advances.text: The trade of the Indies is bound by law to Seville, and the river below the city is hard for laden ships. From 1535 a judge of the Indies sits at Cádiz to clear ships that load and unload there, and others follow in the Canaries. The ports beyond Seville take their share of the trade under the eye of the crown.

advances.name: Mission System
advances.text: Franciscan, Dominican, and Jesuit missionaries established a vast network of missions across the Americas, converting indigenous peoples and extending Spanish cultural influence.

advances.name: Mediterranean Galley Fleet
advances.text: Spain's galeras reales patrolled the Mediterranean, protecting trade routes, fighting Ottoman corsairs, and projecting Aragonese-Catalan power from Barcelona to Naples.

advances.name: Treasure Fleet System
advances.text: The Flota de Indias, organized convoys sailing between Seville, the Caribbean, and the Pacific, constituted the greatest system of transoceanic trade in the early modern world.

event.title: The Treasure Fleet
event.text: Twice each year, the great convoys assemble, the Flota de Indias departing Seville for the ports of Veracruz, Portobelo, and Cartagena, returning laden with the silver of Potosi, the gold of New Granada, the indigo and cochineal of Mexico. The Casa de Contratacion oversees every cargo manifest, every passenger list, every real of silver that passes through Seville's waterfront. This is the greatest organized system of transoceanic trade the world has ever seen. Yet the monopoly that makes it profitable also makes it rigid. Merchants in Cadiz and Barcelona agitate for the right to trade freely with the colonies. Shall we maintain the Crown's iron grip on colonial commerce, maximizing royal revenues but limiting private enterprise, or open the trade to broader participation, accepting lower crown revenues in exchange for a more dynamic economy?

modifiers.name: Crown Treasure Monopoly
modifiers.text: All colonial trade flows through the Casa de Contratacion in Seville. The Crown's monopoly ensures every ounce of silver and every bale of indigo enriches the royal treasury.

modifiers.name: Free Commerce of the Indies
modifiers.text: By loosening the monopoly and permitting wider participation in colonial trade, the commerce of the Indies flows more freely, enriching merchants and manufacturers across Spain.

advances.name: Spanish Galleon
advances.text: The galleon, designed in the 1550s by Pedro Menendez de Aviles and Alvaro de Bazan, combined heavy armament with cargo capacity, serving as both warship and treasure carrier.

advances.name: Potosi Silver Economy
advances.text: The silver mines of Potosi and Zacatecas poured a torrent of precious metal into the Spanish treasury, funding armies and fleets while reshaping the global economy.

advances.name: Manila Galleon Route
advances.text: From 1565, the Manila Galleon linked Acapulco to the Philippines, bringing Chinese silk, porcelain, and spices westward and American silver eastward across the Pacific.

advances.name: Provisioning the Armadas
advances.text: Biscuit, salt pork, wine and cordage for the armadas are bought, stored and loaded by the king's purveyors in the fleet ports, so that a fleet is fitted out in a season and kept at sea for a year.

advances.name: Bourbon Arsenal Reforms
advances.text: The Bourbon dynasty established Royal Factories for arms, shipbuilding, glass, and porcelain, state-sponsored manufactories to modernize Spain's industrial base.

advances.name: Infanteria de Marina
advances.text: Founded in 1537 as the Tercio de Galeras, the Spanish Marine Infantry is the oldest marine corps in the world, fighting aboard warships and in amphibious operations across the globe.

advances.name: Bourbon Centralization
advances.text: The Nueva Planta decrees abolished the separate laws of Aragon, Valencia, and Catalonia, replacing them with Castilian administration and creating a centralized unitary state.

advances.name: Colonial Plantation System
advances.text: Spanish colonial haciendas and plantations produced tobacco, sugar, cacao, and indigo for European markets, sustaining the transatlantic economy.

advances.name: Cadiz Constitution
advances.text: The Constitution of 1812, drafted in besieged Cadiz during the Napoleonic invasion, proclaimed popular sovereignty, separation of powers, and universal male suffrage, a beacon of liberal constitutionalism.

advances.name: Guerrilla Tradition
advances.text: The Peninsular War gave the world the word 'guerrilla', small war. Spanish irregulars harried Napoleon's armies relentlessly, proving that popular resistance could bleed a superpower.

advances.name: Economic Societies
advances.text: The Sociedades Economicas de Amigos del Pais, Economic Societies of Friends of the Country, promoted agricultural improvement, industrial innovation, and scientific education across Spain.

advances.name: Imperial Legacy
advances.text: Three centuries of governing a global empire left Spain with unmatched experience in colonial administration, diplomatic negotiation, and multicontinental governance.

destiny.name: Spanish Destiny
destiny.text: Spain stands at a crossroads. The crown is united and the realm secure, now a greater destiny beckons. Achieve stability and chart the course of the Spanish nation.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: A Crown United
event.text: The kingdoms of Iberia stand united under a single crown. The Reconquista is a living memory, the faith is strong, and Spanish arms are respected throughout Christendom. From the courts of Toledo and Valladolid, from the ports of Barcelona and Seville, the ambitions of a great nation take shape. Whether through the sword of the faithful or the wealth of distant lands, Spain shall leave its mark upon the world.

destiny.name: The Italian Wars
destiny.text: The wealth and prestige of Italy draw Spain into the great power struggle for the peninsula. Seize Naples and Milan to establish Spanish supremacy over Italy.

conditions.text: Chose Universal Monarchy
Own Naples, or a subject owns it
Own Milan, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Prize of Italy
event.text: The banners of Spain fly over Naples and Milan. What generations of Italian princes, French kings, and German emperors struggled to control now rests in Spanish hands. The tercios march through the streets of cities that once answered only to their own lords, and Spanish viceroys administer the richest lands in Europe. Italy is ours, and with it, the key to Mediterranean mastery and European hegemony.

options.text: Italy bows to the Spanish crown.

destiny.name: The Army of Flanders
destiny.text: Spain's reach extends northward. Take Antwerp, heart of the richest provinces in Europe, hold Dole, the seat of Franche-Comté, to keep the Spanish Road open from Milan, and march a great army along it.

conditions.text: Own Antwerp, or a subject owns it
Own Dole, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50
Renaissance or later

event.title: The Army of Flanders
event.text: The Spanish Road, that legendary corridor stretching from Milan through Savoy and Franche-Comte to the Netherlands, now carries a steady stream of men, money, and munitions northward. In Antwerp, the wealthiest city in Europe, Spanish governors oversee a commercial empire that rivals the colonial one. The Army of Flanders, that fearsome instrument of Habsburg power, holds the Low Countries in an iron grip. Yet maintaining this distant army strains even Spain's vast resources. Shall we perfect the military machine, pouring treasure into discipline and fortifications? Or leverage our dynastic connections, using diplomacy to manage what force alone cannot sustain?

options.text: Discipline and steel will hold Flanders.

modifiers.name: Iron Discipline
modifiers.text: The Army of Flanders drills ceaselessly, its garrisons fortified and its recruits hardened by the rigors of northern service, though the domestic economy bears the cost of perpetual war.

options.text: Dynastic ties bind more firmly than iron.

modifiers.name: Habsburg Diplomacy
modifiers.text: Through marriage, alliance, and the careful management of dynastic claims, the Habsburgs weave a web of influence across Europe, though every new commitment draws Spain deeper into costly wars.

destiny.name: Defender of Christendom
destiny.text: Spain aspires to be the universal champion of the Catholic faith. Control Rome, Tunis, and Sicily while maintaining the stability to lead all Christendom.

conditions.text: Own Rome, or a subject owns it
Own Tunis, or a subject owns it
Own Palermo, or a subject owns it
Stability at least 25

event.title: Defender of Christendom
event.text: From the shores of Tunis to the hills of Rome, from the harbors of Sicily to the fortresses of Flanders, Spain's power encircles the Mediterranean and dominates Europe. No king in Christendom commands such armies, no prince defends the faith with such zeal, no realm spans such distances. The dream of a universal Christian monarchy, first glimpsed by Charles V as he knelt before the Pope in Bologna, is within reach. Shall Spain be the champion of Catholic orthodoxy, a crusading power whose armies are the sword of the Church? Or shall we build a Habsburg imperium, a dynasty whose web of alliances and possessions makes it the arbiter of European affairs?

options.text: We are the sword of the Holy Church.

modifiers.name: Catholic Champion
modifiers.text: Spain stands as the armed defender of the Catholic faith, its armies consecrated to the service of the Church, its wars blessed by the Pope himself.

effects.name: Damage Done versus Heathens in Battle

options.text: The House of Habsburg shall rule all.

modifiers.name: Habsburg Imperium
modifiers.text: The Habsburg dynasty sits astride Europe, its prestige unmatched and its diplomatic weight decisive in every negotiation, though the sprawling empire's intellectual life suffers from the demands of governance.

destiny.name: Caribbean Foothold
destiny.text: The New World beckons. Establish a base in Havana and ensure sugar flows through your markets, the first step toward a global colonial empire.

event.title: The Pearl of the Antilles
event.text: Havana stands as the gateway to the New World, a fortress-port where the treasure fleets assemble, where sugar cane sweetens the air, and where the wealth of two continents passes through Spanish hands. From this Caribbean stronghold, the routes fan outward: south to the riches of Peru, west to the silver of Mexico, east to the waiting markets of Seville. The colony is no longer an experiment, it is the foundation of a global empire.

destiny.name: The Pacific Link
destiny.text: From Mexico to Manila, forge the greatest trade route the world has ever seen. Control Tenochtitlan and Manila, and let the galleon trade grow Manila into a city, linking the wealth of Asia to the Americas.

conditions.text: Own Tenōchtitlan, or a subject owns it
Own Maynila, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Manila Galleon
event.text: The impossible has been achieved. Spanish ships now cross the Pacific, linking the silver of Mexico to the silk and spices of Asia. In Manila, Chinese junks crowd the harbor alongside Spanish galleons, trading porcelain and lacquerware for American silver. In Acapulco, the annual arrival of the Manila Galleon triggers a frenzy of commerce that draws merchants from across the Americas. No other nation has forged such a link, a single trading route that girdles the globe. Shall the crown tighten its grip on this oceanic monopoly, building a fleet that dominates the Pacific? Or shall we open the ports, letting private enterprise multiply the wealth that flows along this remarkable route?

options.text: The crown controls the Pacific trade.

modifiers.name: Crown Fleet
modifiers.text: The royal fleet dominates the Pacific sea lanes, its blockades choking rivals and its traditions of seamanship unmatched, though the crown's obsession with oceanic trade draws resources from the homeland.

options.text: Open the ports to all who would trade.

modifiers.name: Free Ports of the Indies
modifiers.text: By opening colonial ports to broader commerce, raw materials flow freely and merchants prosper, though the standing army, starved of monopoly revenues, grows costlier to maintain.

destiny.name: The Global Empire
destiny.text: Complete the conquest of the greatest indigenous empire in the Americas. Every fleet of the Indies sails from Seville and returns to it, and the city on the Guadalquivir is built up to twice what it was; the silver it lands is struck into pieces of eight. Requires Cusco, Seville at 75 development and a Silver Minting House in three places.

event.title: The Empire on Which the Sun Never Sets
event.text: From the Andes to the Philippines, from the Caribbean to the Mediterranean, the Spanish Empire spans every continent and every ocean. The ancient cities of the Incas now fly the banner of Castile, and in every corner of this vast dominion, Spanish law, Spanish faith, and Spanish language take root. No empire in history has governed such diversity of peoples across such distances. Shall we centralize this colossus through a system of viceroyalties and audiencias, binding the empire together with uniform law and administration? Or shall we let the silver that flows from Potosi and Zacatecas become the foundation of Spanish economic power, investing the wealth of empire in fleets, fortifications, and public works?

options.text: One law, one faith, one empire.

modifiers.name: Centralized Viceroyalties
modifiers.text: A system of viceroys, audiencias, and intendants binds the empire under uniform law. Colonial populations are integrated, local officials answer to the crown, and administrative efficiency reaches new heights.

modifiers.name: Silver Standard
modifiers.text: The wealth of Potosi and Zacatecas flows into warships, fortifications, and public works. Silver funds a navy that dominates the oceans and an army larger than any rival can match.

units.name: Rodelero
units.text: Sword-and-buckler infantry, fierce close-combat fighters who charged into pike formations to hack at the enemy at close quarters, a tradition born in the Reconquista.

units.name: Jinete
units.text: Light cavalrymen riding a la jineta, short stirrups, light lances, round shields, the heirs of an Iberian equestrian tradition shared between Christian and Moorish horsemen.

units.name: Tercio
units.text: Spain's legendary combined-arms infantry formation: pikemen, swordsmen, and arquebusiers fighting as a disciplined whole. The terror of Europe's battlefields for over a century.

units.name: Galera Real
units.text: A royal war galley of the Spanish Mediterranean fleet, heavier and more heavily armed than standard galleys, carrying soldier complements for boarding actions.

units.name: Spanish Galleon
units.text: A heavily armed sailing warship designed to escort treasure convoys across the Atlantic, combining formidable broadside firepower with substantial cargo capacity.

units.name: Infanteria de Marina
units.text: The oldest marine infantry corps in the world, descended from the Tercio de Galeras. Specialists in shipboard combat and amphibious assault.

buildings.name: Alcazar
buildings.text: A fortified palace combining military defense with royal administration, the architectural legacy of centuries of frontier warfare between Christian and Moorish kingdoms.

buildings.name: Esquileo
buildings.text: A shearing house beside a royal drove road. The merino flocks are shorn here in spring on their way to the summer pastures of the north, and the fleeces are sorted, washed and baled for the fairs.

buildings.name: Colonial Mission
buildings.text: A Franciscan or Dominican mission compound, church, school, workshop, and dormitory, established to convert and educate indigenous peoples in the Spanish Americas.

buildings.name: Juzgado de Indias
buildings.text: The court of a judge of the Indies in a port outside Seville. Ships bound for the Indies are registered here, their cargoes inspected and the crown's dues collected, so that they need not go up the river.

buildings.name: Proveeduria de Armadas
buildings.text: The yard of the purveyor general in a fleet port. Hemp, pitch and canvas are bought on contract and kept in the king's stores beside the quay, next to the ovens that bake the ship's biscuit.

buildings.name: Silver Minting House
buildings.text: A royal mint processing colonial silver into coin, the reales de a ocho, pieces of eight, that became the first truly global currency.

buildings.name: Royal Foundry
buildings.text: A state-sponsored manufactory established under Bourbon reforms, casting cannon, forging arms, and producing the materiel that sustains Spain's military power.

buildings.name: Camino Real
buildings.text: The Royal Road, part of Charles III's radial road system connecting Madrid to every major city, improving trade, communication, and administration across the kingdom.

buildings.name: El Escorial
buildings.text: The great monastery-palace of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, simultaneously royal residence, monastery, library, and mausoleum, the architectural embodiment of Spain's claim to be the defender of Christendom.

buildings.name: Real Audiencia
buildings.text: A Royal Court of Appeals, the supreme judicial and administrative institution of colonial governance, enforcing Spanish law and the rights of the crown across the vast territories of the Indies.

list.name: Colegios Mayores
list.text: The six Colegios Mayores were endowed to lodge poor scholars of law and theology: San Bartolomé at Salamanca in 1401, three more in the same city, Santa Cruz at Valladolid and San Ildefonso at Alcalá. Their graduates came to fill the councils, the high courts and the bishoprics of the monarchy, and each college kept a network of former fellows who advanced its men. The crown gained a standing reserve of trained letrados. By the seventeenth century the colleges had become closed circles of well-born families, which the reform of 1771 finally broke.

list.name: Consulado de Cargadores a Indias
list.text: Chartered in 1543, the Consulado de Cargadores a Indias was the guild of the Seville merchants who shipped to the Indies. Its prior and consuls judged commercial suits, organised the lading of the fleets, and came to farm the avería, the levy that paid for the convoy escorts. The crown borrowed from the guild constantly and confirmed its monopoly in return. The guild defended that monopoly against Cádiz, against foreign houses and against the merchants of Mexico and Lima, long after it had ceased to serve the trade.

conditions.text: Owns Sevilla

list.name: Consejo de Indias
list.text: Created by Charles V in 1524 on the conciliar model of the Council of Castile, the Council of the Indies governed Spain's overseas empire from Madrid until 1834. Its six to ten royal appointees drafted all colonial legislation, named viceroys and audiencia magistrates, audited the residencias of departing governors, and sat as the supreme court of appeal for the New World. No major undertaking in the Indies (a campaign, a reform, an ecclesiastical appointment) proceeded without its written consulta to the king.

conditions.text: A subject or a subject's subject

list.name: Maestranzas de Caballería
list.text: The Real Maestranza de Caballería of Ronda was founded in 1573, after Philip II asked the nobility of the towns to form brotherhoods that would keep them practised in horsemanship and arms. Seville followed in 1670, Granada in 1686 and Valencia in 1697. The maestrantes drilled in the riding school and the bullring, and bred and schooled horses for the cavalry. Under the Bourbons they won a royal prince as elder brother and a jurisdiction of their own, which put them beyond the reach of the ordinary magistrates.

list.name: Tribunal del Santo Oficio
list.text: Authorised by Sixtus IV in 1478 and inaugurated by the Catholic Monarchs in 1480, the Holy Office of the Inquisition operated outside papal control through fourteen local tribunals across Castile, Aragon, and the Indies. Crown-appointed inquisitors enforced the orthodoxy of conversos and moriscos, tried witches and humanist scholars, censored the press through the Index, and conducted the auto-da-fé as a public theatre of monarchical authority. Property confiscations from the condemned filled the royal treasury, but the institution corroded the converso commercial networks on which Castilian trade had relied and chilled the open intellectual life of the Spanish universities.

conditions.text: Catholicism religion

list.name: Encomienda
list.text: Defined in law in 1503, the encomienda granted a conquistador or settler the right to collect tribute and labour from a specified Indian community in exchange for protection and Christian instruction. The system planted a Spanish lordly class in the New World almost overnight, but Las Casas's denunciations and the Valladolid debate forced Charles V to promulgate the New Laws of 1542 forbidding new grants and abolishing inheritance. Colonial revolt (the assassination of Viceroy Núñez Vela in Peru) postponed enforcement, and the encomienda decayed into the rotational repartimiento: a labour draft administered by the crown but everywhere abused by local officials and parish priests.

conditions.text: A subject or a subject's subject

list.name: Corregimiento
list.text: Royal magistrates appointed to the municipalities of Castile from 1480 onwards, the corregidores were drawn exclusively from non-noble letrados of the law schools. Each corregidor presided over the cabildo, tried cases of first instance, collected royal taxes, and policed the boundary between crown jurisdiction and the immunities of church, seigneur, and chartered town. After the suppression of the comuneros revolt of 1520-21, the corregimiento became the principal lever by which the Habsburg crown broke municipal autonomy and absorbed the older cities of Old Castile into the unitary administration of the realm.
